problem:
The canonical record is Question 5.6.1 in Keith Burns and Vladimir S. Matveev's problem list. After checking the original PDF, the recoverable statement is:

> **Question 5.6.1 (Miller, Reid).** Are there infinitely many simple closed geodesics in every hyperbolic three-manifold of finite volume?

The genuine commentary continues:

> One can ask the same question for manifolds of variable negative curvature in any dimension. The answer is positive for surfaces, since in this case a free homotopy class contains a simple closed geodesic if and only if it contains a simple closed curve. The answer is also positive for generic metrics of negative curvature. Reid has examples of (arithmetic) hyperbolic manifolds of finite volume in which every closed geodesic is simple.

Two extraction defects were removed, without changing mathematical content.

1. The page header “OPEN PROBLEMS AND QUESTIONS ABOUT GEODESICS 13” interrupts the phrase “free homotopy class” in the extracted record.
2. Everything beginning with “6. Nonpositive curvature and non uniform hyperbolicity of the geodesic flow” belongs to the next section. The rank, Jacobi-field, and ergodicity material is not part of Question 5.6.1.

The last sentence also compresses its attribution: the cited 1993 paper is by **Ted Chinburg and Alan W. Reid**, not Reid alone. Its title uses “all closed geodesics,” but the mathematically coherent and later explicit formulation is “all **primitive** closed geodesics are simple”; see Section 3 below.
status_literature:
**Status as checked on 2026-08-08: partially solved, with the closed case still open.**

- Adams, Hass, and Scott proved that every complete nonelementary orientable hyperbolic 3-manifold, except the 3-dimensional Fuchsian quotient associated with the thrice-punctured sphere, contains at least one simple closed geodesic. In particular, every orientable finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold contains one.
- Miller studied geodesic knots in the figure-eight knot complement and arithmetic families. The arithmetic statements sometimes concern quotients described as orbifolds; a torsion-free hypothesis is needed before treating such a quotient as a manifold.
- Chinburg and Reid constructed infinitely many mutually incommensurable **closed arithmetic hyperbolic 3-manifolds** in which every primitive closed geodesic is simple. These are strong positive examples, not a proof for all manifolds.
- Kuhlmann proved in 2006 that every **cusped orientable** finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold contains infinitely many simple closed geodesics. Her 2008 paper gave checkable geometric and arithmetic sufficient conditions in the **closed orientable** case. The current K3 problem list reports that these conditions were verified for 178 of the first 200 closed manifolds in the census.
- Xia's 2021 preprint extended the cusp argument to manifolds with a virtually rank-two cusp and, in particular, to **every cusped finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold**, including the nonorientable case.
- Xia explicitly states that it remains unknown whether every closed hyperbolic 3-manifold has infinitely many simple closed geodesics. The 2026 AMS volume *K3: A New Problem List in Low-Dimensional Topology* retains exactly this question as Problem 3.16 and separately summarizes the cusped and conditional closed results.

Consequently, for the usual meaning of “finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold,” the original question is now equivalent to its **closed** subcase: the noncompact finite-volume (cusped) subcase is known. I found no primary-source announcement through the search date that settles every closed manifold.

### 3. Definitions and assumptions

#### Manifold, not orbifold

Here a hyperbolic 3-manifold is a complete quotient

\[
M=\mathbb H^3/\Gamma
\]

where \(\Gamma<\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb H^3)\) is discrete, torsion-free, and acts freely. Orientability is not built into the definition unless explicitly stated. If \(\Gamma\) has torsion, the quotient is an orbifold and is outside the statement being analyzed. The new results below also use freeness and are not asserted verbatim for orbifolds.

#### Geometric simplicity and primitivity

A **simple closed geodesic** means an embedded geometric circle \(C\subset M\) that is geodesic. Equivalently, its once-around parametrization \(S^1\to M\) is injective. Distinct geodesics are counted by distinct unoriented images, or equivalently by primitive loxodromic conjugacy classes up to inversion.

If a closed geodesic parametrization is traversed \(k>1\) times, it is not injective, but its underlying image can still be an embedded circle. Thus iterations do not create new simple geodesics. The literal statement “every parametrized closed geodesic is simple” is impossible in any manifold containing a closed geodesic, since its second iterate is noninjective. This is why the Chinburg--Reid statement must be read, as Xia reads it, as a statement about primitive closed geodesics or geometric images.

For an axial element \(a\in\Gamma\), write \(A_a\subset\mathbb H^3\) for its invariant axis. The stabilizer of this axis is infinite cyclic:

\[
\operatorname{Stab}_{\Gamma}(A_a)=\langle r\rangle.
\]

The element \(r\) is the primitive root along that axis; if \(a=r^k\), then the orbit parametrized by \(a\) traverses the geometric circle \(\pi(A_a)\) \(|k|\) times.

#### Closed versus cusped

A finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold is either closed or has finitely many cusps. Kuhlmann and Xia settle the cusped case. The unresolved portion is therefore the existence of infinitely many embedded primitive geodesic images in every closed hyperbolic 3-manifold.

### 4. Approach map

The investigation used three routes.

1. **Source recovery and status audit.** Separate the actual Section 5.6 text from Section 6 spill, then compare the 1993, 2001, 2006, 2008, 2021, and 2026 sources.
2. **Universal-cover criterion.** Translate self-intersection into intersection of distinct translates of one axis in \(\mathbb H^3\).
3. **Finite-cover analysis.** Determine exactly when a simple geodesic in a finite cover remains simple downstairs. This isolates why virtual results about hyperbolic 3-manifolds do not automatically solve the closed case.

The first route establishes the current boundary. The second and third give the proved candidate contribution.

### 7. Detailed proof, derivation, or heuristic

#### Proof of Lemma 5.1

Let \(A\cong\mathbb R\) be the axis of \(a\). Restriction to \(A\) gives a homomorphism

\[
\rho:\operatorname{Stab}_{\Gamma}(A)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Isom}(A).
\]

Its kernel fixes every point of \(A\). Since \(\Gamma\) acts freely on \(\mathbb H^3\), that kernel is trivial. An element of \(\operatorname{Isom}(A)\) reversing the orientation of \(A\) has a fixed point on \(A\), so no nontrivial element in the image of \(\rho\) can be a reflection. Hence the image consists of translations. Their translation lengths form a discrete subgroup of \((\mathbb R,+)\): otherwise lengths tending to zero, together with compactness of the rotational factor about \(A\), would produce nonidentity elements of \(\Gamma\) tending to the identity, contradicting discreteness. The image is therefore generated by one least positive translation. Thus \(\operatorname{Stab}_{\Gamma}(A)=\langle r\rangle\), with \(r\) primitive.

The map \(A/\langle r\rangle\to M\) is an immersed geodesic circle. Suppose that \(gA\) meets \(A\) for some \(g\notin\operatorname{Stab}_{\Gamma}(A)\). The two geodesic lines are distinct. Distinct geodesics in \(\mathbb H^3\) that meet have different tangent lines at their meeting point; otherwise uniqueness for the geodesic initial-value problem would make them equal. Their projections therefore give two distinct local branches of \(C\) through one point, so \(C\) is not embedded.

Conversely, suppose (5.1) holds. If two points \(x,y\in A\) have the same image in \(M\), then \(y=gx\) for some \(g\in\Gamma\). Hence \(A\cap gA\ne\varnothing\), so (5.1) forces \(g\in\operatorname{Stab}_{\Gamma}(A)\). Therefore \(x\) and \(y\) already represent the same point of \(A/\langle r\rangle\). The induced map \(A/\langle r\rangle\to M\) is injective. Since its domain is compact and \(M\) is Hausdorff, it is an embedding. This proves the criterion.

Finally, replacing \(r\) by \(a=r^k\) does not change \(A\) or its image. It changes only the parametrization degree. This proves the last assertion.

#### Proof of Theorem 5.2

The full preimage of \(p(C)\) contains the finite union

\[
U=\bigcup_{d\in D}dC.
\]

Assume (5.2). Distinct members of this union are disjoint, while the elements of \(D_C\) preserve \(C\). Thus the restriction of the quotient by \(D\) to this union identifies \(p(C)\) with \(C/D_C\). Deck transformations act freely on \(N\), so \(D_C\) acts freely on the circle \(C\). A finite free action on a circle is by rotations after choosing the arclength coordinate. Therefore \(C/D_C\) is a circle, the quotient map has degree \(|D_C|\), and the local-isometry property of \(p\) gives (5.3). The resulting circle in \(M\) is embedded.

Conversely, suppose some \(dC\) meets \(C\) but \(dC\ne C\). At an intersection point the two closed geodesics have different tangent lines, since equality of tangent data would force equality of the entire geodesics. Their images under the local isometry \(p\) become two different branches of \(p(C)\) through the same point. Hence \(p(C)\) is not embedded. This proves necessity and sufficiency.

#### Proof of Corollary 5.3

Because \(D\) is finite and each \(\mathcal B_d\) is finite, the union

\[
\mathcal B=\bigcup_{d\in D}\mathcal B_d
\]

is finite. Every \(C\in\mathcal C\setminus\mathcal B\) satisfies (5.2), so Theorem 5.2 says that \(p(C)\) is embedded.

It remains to rule out collapse of infinitely many upstairs circles to finitely many downstairs circles. For a fixed embedded geodesic \(G\subset M\), every embedded geodesic \(C\subset N\) satisfying \(p(C)=G\) is a connected component of \(p^{-1}(G)\). A degree-\(|D|\) cover has at most \(|D|\) such components. Thus each downstairs image accounts for only finitely many members of \(\mathcal C\), and the infinitely many good members have infinitely many distinct images.

For the contrapositive, if only finitely many simple images exist downstairs, then the union of the bad sets cannot be finite. Since \(D\) is finite, at least one \(\mathcal B_d\) is infinite. The identity never belongs to a bad set, so this \(d\) is nontrivial.

#### Upward permanence

For completeness, let \(q:Y\to X\) be any finite Riemannian cover, not necessarily regular. If \(G\subset X\) is an embedded closed geodesic, then each component of \(q^{-1}(G)\) is an embedded circle and is geodesic because \(q\) is a local isometry. Distinct base geodesics have disjoint labels as subsets and cannot share one lift component. Therefore infinitely many simple closed geodesics in \(X\) give infinitely many in \(Y\). This direction needs no deck-group condition.

### 8. Verification and attempted falsification

Several edge cases were checked explicitly.

1. **Iterates.** If \(a=r^k\), \(k>1\), then the parametrized orbit of \(a\) is not simple. Lemma 5.1 speaks about the geometric image and explicitly records the primitive root, so it does not make the impossible claim that iterates are injective.
2. **Axis normalization.** The correct exception in (5.1) is the full axis stabilizer, not merely \(\langle a\rangle\). If \(a\) is a proper power, using only \(\langle a\rangle\) would falsely treat the primitive root as producing a self-intersection.
3. **Deck stabilizers.** In (5.2), a nonidentity \(d\) may preserve \(C\). This is not a self-intersection; it makes \(C\) cover a shorter embedded circle. Excluding all nonidentity intersections would be too strong.
4. **Proper intersections.** Two distinct geodesics cannot be tangent at an intersection point. Thus a proper translate intersection really produces two local branches downstairs.
5. **Two-sheeted sanity check.** For a regular double cover with involution \(\iota\), the criterion reduces to exactly three possibilities: \(\iota C=C\) (embedded image, degree two), \(\iota C\cap C=\varnothing\) (embedded image, degree one), or a proper intersection (nonsimple image). This exhausts the geometry.
6. **Distinctness downstairs.** Infinite \(\mathcal C\) cannot collapse to one embedded geodesic because the preimage of one circle under a finite cover has finitely many components.
7. **Cusps.** The proofs use only covering geometry and proper discontinuity, not compactness. They apply to both closed and cusped manifolds, although the global question is already settled in the cusped case.
8. **Nonorientability.** The covering statements do not require orientability. The axis-stabilizer proof uses freeness; an isometry reversing an axis would fix a point on it and therefore cannot occur in the stabilizer of a freely acting group.
9. **Orbifolds.** If torsion is allowed, an axis stabilizer can contain rotations fixing the axis and the free-action arguments fail. No orbifold extension is claimed.
10. **Global gap.** No finite cover with a suitable infinite family is constructed for an arbitrary closed hyperbolic 3-manifold. The reduction therefore does not solve Question 5.6.1.

No computation was used beyond inspecting JSON/source text and checking bibliographic metadata.

### 5. Main result

#### Lemma 5.1 (axis-stabilizer and embedding criterion)

Let \(M=\mathbb H^3/\Gamma\) be a hyperbolic manifold and let \(a\in\Gamma\) be axial with axis \(A=A_a\). Then \(\operatorname{Stab}_{\Gamma}(A)=\langle r\rangle\) for a primitive axial element \(r\), and the geometric closed geodesic \(C=\pi(A)\) is embedded if and only if

\[
A\cap gA=\varnothing
\qquad\text{for every }g\in\Gamma\setminus\operatorname{Stab}_{\Gamma}(A).
\tag{5.1}
\]

Thus simplicity is a translate-disjointness condition; it is independent of whether the chosen element \(a=r^k\) parametrizes the image once or repeatedly.

#### Theorem 5.2 (exact finite-cover descent criterion)

Let \(p:N\to M\) be a finite regular Riemannian covering with finite deck group \(D\), and let \(C\subset N\) be an embedded closed geodesic image. Put

\[
D_C=\{d\in D:dC=C\}.
\]

Then \(p(C)\) is an embedded closed geodesic image in \(M\) if and only if

\[
\text{for every }d\in D,\qquad dC=C\quad\text{or}\quad dC\cap C=\varnothing.
\tag{5.2}
\]

When (5.2) holds, \(p|_C:C\to p(C)\) has degree \(|D_C|\), and

\[
\ell(p(C))=\frac{\ell(C)}{|D_C|},
\tag{5.3}
\]

where both lengths refer to once-around geometric circles. In particular, \(dC=C\) is not an obstruction to an embedded **image**; it only says that the chosen upstairs circle covers a shorter circle downstairs.

#### Corollary 5.3 (finite-deck obstruction principle)

Let \(\mathcal C\) be an infinite set of distinct embedded closed geodesic images in \(N\). For \(d\in D\), define

\[
\mathcal B_d=
\{C\in\mathcal C:C\cap dC\ne\varnothing\text{ and }dC\ne C\}.
\]

If every \(\mathcal B_d\) is finite, then \(M\) contains infinitely many simple closed geodesics. Equivalently, if \(N\) has infinitely many simple closed geodesics but \(M\) has only finitely many, then for each chosen infinite upstairs family \(\mathcal C\), some nonidentity deck transformation \(d\) (which may depend on \(\mathcal C\)) properly intersects infinitely many members of that family.

The property “contains infinitely many simple closed geodesics” always passes **up** a finite cover, but Corollary 5.3 identifies the exact obstruction to passing it **down** a regular finite cover.

### 6. Candidate novel contribution

**Candidate contribution (proved reduction; low novelty confidence).** In a finite regular cover \(N\to M\), failure of an infinite family of simple geodesics to yield infinitely many simple geodesics downstairs forces a single nontrivial deck transformation to properly intersect infinitely many members of that family. The pointwise criterion (5.2), the degree formula (5.3), and the finite-pigeonhole conclusion are packaged together as the finite-deck obstruction principle.

This claim is explicit and testable: for a geometrically constructed family \(C_n\subset N\), there are only finitely many deck transformations, and one can try to prove for each \(d\ne 1\) that \(C_n\cap dC_n=\varnothing\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), unless \(dC_n=C_n\). If successful, infinitude descends.

Why it may be useful: modern virtual methods often replace a closed hyperbolic 3-manifold by a finite cover, but an embedded curve upstairs can project to a self-intersecting curve. The criterion isolates precisely the extra geometric input needed to turn an upstairs construction into a result downstairs.

Literature checked: Burns--Matveev; Adams--Hass--Scott; Chinburg--Reid; Miller; Kuhlmann's 2006 and 2008 papers; Xia; and the 2026 K3 problem list. I did not find this exact finite-family/pigeonhole formulation in those sources. It is nevertheless an elementary covering-space consequence and may be standard folklore. Therefore the novelty confidence is **low**, not a claim of global originality.
what_remains:
### 9. Limitations and unresolved gaps

- The universal closed-manifold case remains open.
- Corollary 5.3 is a reduction, not an existence theorem: one still needs an infinite family upstairs and uniform control of its intersections with every deck translate.
- A generic finite cover can create exactly the obstruction described; virtual fibering, residual finiteness, or the existence of embedded objects in a cover does not by itself establish descent.
- The status search emphasized the primary papers and the 2026 K3 problem list. It was not a citation-exhaustive database review, so the candidate novelty is deliberately labeled low-confidence.
- The original commentary's broader question for variable negative curvature and arbitrary dimension was not attacked. The proved covering statements remain true for Riemannian coverings in any dimension, but the global existence problem can behave differently.

### 10. Concrete next steps

1. Start with a closed manifold \(M\) and a regular finite cover \(N\) satisfying one of Kuhlmann's sufficient conditions. Apply her spiraling construction equivariantly and estimate \(C_n\cap dC_n\) for every \(d\in D\).
2. In the universal cover, choose axes \(A_n\) for the constructed family. For a representative of each nontrivial deck class, reduce proper intersection to checking whether \(A_n\) meets one of finitely many coset families \(g\Lambda A_n\). A limiting-axis separation lemma would verify Corollary 5.3.
3. Test the double-cover case first. It requires control of only one involution and cleanly distinguishes invariant, disjoint, and crossing families.
4. Search specifically for closed manifolds not covered by Kuhlmann's known census verification, and determine whether the obstruction is geometric failure of her hypotheses or only failure of the available certification.
5. If an arbitrary finite cover rather than a regular one is natural, pass to its normal core. Simple geodesics lift to the normal refinement; then apply the finite-deck criterion to the regular composite cover.

### References

1. K. Burns and V. S. Matveev, “Open problems and questions about geodesics,” *Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems* **41** (2021), 641–684. DOI: [10.1017/etds.2019.73](https://doi.org/10.1017/etds.2019.73). Original AIM PDF: <https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf>.
2. C. Adams, J. Hass, and P. Scott, “Simple closed geodesics in hyperbolic 3-manifolds,” *Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society* **31** (1999), 81–86. DOI: [10.1112/S0024609398004883](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0024609398004883); arXiv: [math/9801071](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9801071).
3. T. Chinburg and A. W. Reid, “Closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds whose closed geodesics all are simple,” *Journal of Differential Geometry* **38** (1993), 545–558, MR1243786. Bibliographic confirmation on [Alan Reid's publication list](https://web.ma.utexas.edu/users/areid/publications.html).
4. K. N. Jones and A. W. Reid, “Non-simple geodesics in hyperbolic 3-manifolds,” *Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society* **116** (1994), 339–351. DOI: [10.1017/S0305004100072625](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100072625).
5. S. M. Miller, “Geodesic knots in the figure-eight knot complement,” *Experimental Mathematics* **10** (2001), 419–436. DOI: [10.1080/10586458.2001.10504460](https://doi.org/10.1080/10586458.2001.10504460).
6. S. M. Kuhlmann, “Geodesic knots in cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds,” *Algebraic & Geometric Topology* **6** (2006), 2151–2162. DOI: [10.2140/agt.2006.6.2151](https://doi.org/10.2140/agt.2006.6.2151).
7. S. M. Kuhlmann, “Geodesic knots in closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds,” *Geometriae Dedicata* **131** (2008), 181–211. DOI: [10.1007/s10711-007-9227-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10711-007-9227-8).
8. F. Xia, “Simple closed geodesics in cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds,” arXiv: [2110.14376](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14376), 2021.
9. R. İnanç Baykur, R. C. Kirby, and D. Ruberman (eds.), *K3: A New Problem List in Low-Dimensional Topology*, Mathematical Surveys and Monographs 295, American Mathematical Society, 2026, Problem 3.16. [AMS book page](https://bookstore.ams.org/SURV/295).

Recall that the rank of a vector v in such a manifold is the dimension of the space of Jacobi fields along the geodesic γv that are covariantly constant. It is easily seen that rank is upper semi continuous. All vectors have rank ≥ 1, since the velocity vector field is a covariantly constant Jacobi field.
